March 2011 # A consumers’ strike - The LME 3-month copper price hit $10,160/t on 14th February, driven by positive economic news and sustained Chinese imports. Prices then dropped by more than 3% in two days late in the month, as market sentiment was dampened by the unrest in Africa & the Middle East and fears related to higher oil prices. - Consumers are largely covered at the moment through contracted material. A high price and tight credit is leading to a working capital squeeze on fabricators and limited spot buying interest. This is another sign of on-going price-driven demand destruction. Exchange inventories continue to rise while merchant premia decline. - Supported by ongoing increases in collection rates (including theft) globally, the scrap market remains well-supplied and could weigh more heavily on spot cathode demand once spot buying interest does resume. |The supply/demand

# $10,000/t copper... Copper prices have hit a series of new records in the past few weeks, driven by the belief that the cathode market will be in a substantial deficit this year. Further support has come from a string of positive news on the underlying economy, especially from the industrialised world. The ISM’s Purchasing Manager Index (PMI) in the US rose to 60.8% in January, its highest level since April 2004, as new orders expanded robustly. The Markit Eurozone Manufacturing PMI also improved from 57.1 in December to 57.3 in January, with 8 major economies seeing growth, except for Greece. German luxury car production and exports have performed particularly strongly. In response, the LME 3-month price advanced by more than 5% in one week and hit a record high of $10,126/t on 7th February. Nevertheless, China tightened credit further by raising its interest rate **5500 Feb-10 May-10 Aug-10 Nov-10** by 25 basis points on 8th February. The US dollar strengthened and demand worries resurfaced, pushing the price down to a low of Data: LME $9,865/t on 10th February. This trend was quickly reversed on 14th February when the price rose to $10,160/t as preliminary data showed that Chinese imports of wrought and unwrought copper rose by 5.7% to 364,240t in January. It then fell back over inflation concerns in China as the latest CPI (which does not include food prices) increased by 4.9% in January. Nervousness built up after the government raised the reserve ratio on 18th February for the second time this year to curb inflation. The price initially found support around $9,800/t. At the time of writing, prices have fallen again to threaten $9,300/t on a reversal in risk appetite due to the ongoing North African and Middle East political crisis, and economic fears from higher oil prices. #### …means higher working capital for consumers Consumers booked in higher proportions of their requirements than last year and are therefore less likely to need to tap into the spot market. However, the high copper price is suppressing global physical market activity despite support from strong underlying industrial production growth. Downstream market participants in the copper chain, particularly in North America and Europe, are feeling the pressure. Fabricators’ margins decline m-o-m as copper edges higher, given that the ‘easier cost cutting measures’ were already taken during the worst time of the recession. Spot material is being ordered on a strictly hand-to-mouth basis and there is not much scope for further expenditure reduction. There has also been a growing concern about rising costs for

other inputs weighing on cash flows.  It was reported that some major semis manufacturers, including Wieland Werke (Germany), Luvata (worldwide) and Hussey Copper (US) have been requesting faster payments from their customers in order to minimise the burden of the high copper price on cash flows in the last six months. Most recently, copper wirerod producer Elektrokoppar announced that it would cut one shift and reduce output by some 20%, compared to the previous year, and sales would now only cover Northern Europe.  The Swedish fabricator said it incurs high freight rates selling to other parts of Europe for marginally profitable business. Financing costs are high especially when copper is trading around $10,000/t.  The company also stressed that ‘it has been a necessity to shorten payment terms’ with its customers and ‘fabricators cannot act as bankers’. This is an example of the credit squeeze from banks not extending every loan facility for working capital to cover the additional costs due to the higher copper price.  So, even if orders are improving, some fabricators are finding it difficult to get the credit lines they need to purchase additional raw materials.  This is another sign of the process of demand destruction from the rationing effect of the high copper price.  As a result, consumers are unwillingly destocking, leading to higher stocks at exchanges and easier availability in the physical market. If larger fabricators are publicising these moves, then other smaller players will be under even greater pressure.

High working capital costs as a result of high prices are limiting buying ability.  As a result, spot activity in Europe has remained slow in February.  The range of quoted merchant premia has remained largely the same at around $50-90/t, though with more deals being concluded at the lower end.  Cathode stocks at both wirerod mills and brass mills remain low, as they hold only what is strictly necessary to meet the immediate orders on their books.  A major European wirerod fabricator said that it has been a good year, driven by a recovery in enamelled wire demand for transformers and motors in Europe, possibly an effect of previous national stimulus packages.  However, it too has been aggressive on reducing payment terms (to around 7 days) because copper is expensive, and will not deliver to customers who do not comply with the requirement. 

Like Europe, the US market has been quiet over the last month and the high copper price has deterred any uptick in the spot market, especially when most semis fabricators are covered with contracted material.  Spot premiums quoted in the US are largely unchanged from January because very few deals were closed in North America.  US-based cable manufacturer General Cable said that its margins remain squeezed even though it expects sales and revenue to increase in Q1 this year.

Demand is too soft to fully pass on rising raw material prices, which account for 85% of its manufacturing costs. Winter storms across the USA also meant that some fabricators lost production days and minor logistics issues were reported. In contrast, the magnet wire business is picking up, thanks to improved demand for electric motors from the home appliance and automotive sectors, due to better consumer confidence. However, this is a smaller market for copper, making up only around 10% of total consumption. Slow semis demand and the reluctance to stock cathode are illustrated by the movement of COMEX and LME stocks in the US, which have resumed an upward trend since the end of January. Although, with doubts rising as to whether the proposed new physical ETFs are actually going to get off the ground, questions (which it is too soon to answer) have been raised as to whether any of this stock rise is due to off warrant metal bought in preparation for the ETFs coming back on warrant. #### China is not immune In China, SHFE inventory rose to 161,062t on 18th February, compared to 129,250t at the end of January, and the Shanghai physical market discount widened to RMB400-500/t lately, indicating a well supplied physical market. The Lantern Festival marked the end of the Lunar New Year celebration and most semis producers have now returned to operation. However, the elevated and volatile copper price has constrained buying interest in the Chinese spot market. Spot premiums are currently being quoted as low as $0-50/t, compared to $30-60/t in January. Consumers are reluctant to make any additional purchases and have chosen to wait for the copper price to fall. Operating rates of semis plants in February are slightly down on January due to the holidays and overall consumption is weaker than expected. There are concerns about further credit tightening as inflation control has become a priority for the government. We believe the sustained -40 2008 2009 2010 level of imports in January was partly linked to financing deals in Data: GTIS, CRU China. These deals use imported copper as collateral to obtain funds for re-lending or financing other corporate developments that offer greater profits. Refined imports rose 7.4% m-o-m in January, but net imports were only 2% higher due to the increase in LME/SHFE arbitrage trade that saw exports double as metal was shipped to LME warehouses in nearby countries, particularly Korea, Singapore and Malaysia. CRU estimates that cathode held in bonded warehouses in Shanghai has now risen to around 500,000t, compared to 300,000t in November 2010. The working capital squeeze also applies in China, and this partly explains why Chinese cop

#### Scrap is not selling either As the world’s largest net importer, China is the swing market for cathode and scrap. The market is not only well supplied with cathode, but also scrap. CRU believes that Chinese importers had built up their scrap stocks in December ahead of the VAT rebate cancellation deadline on 31st December 2010. Imports retreated m-o-m to 365,000t in January, according to customs data. On a global level, scrap traders report that it is very difficult to sell because of the high availability and the lack of Chinese buying interest in the market, mainly due to the negative arbitrage between SHFE and the LME. As industrial production continues to recover, scrap generation follows suit due to increased collection of scrap globally, with tonnages moving quickly through the supply chain and swelling inventories. Fabricators generally lose out to smelters in buying scrap, as the latter are prepared to pay higher prices. Brass mills, however, have already switched to using more scrap to, for instance, as high as 80% of contained copper input in Italy. Therefore, scope for consumers outside of China to boost scrap consumption is limited and should have only a minimal negative impact on cathode demand. European smelters are fully covered for Q1 and concentrates are generally preferred to scrap because of technical issues, as well as the high price of scrap. The chart above shows that scrap prices currently are around $8,500/t, a level the price of cathode has not seen since August 2010. Thus, until Chinese scrap buying increases, scrap availability should remain high and so will discounts. This bodes ill for cathode demand once Chinese buying does pick up though, as cheaper scrap is likely to be preferred to refined metal by those semis producers who can use it. #### Miners earning huge profits While semis producers are suffering, miners are profiting handsomely. Many second half results are in and we estimate refined output in Q4 2010 was up 1.3% q-o-q due to improved utilisation rates and availability of raw materials. Mining companies have reported record profits thanks to the ongoing boom in metal prices. BHP Billiton reported first half net profit of $10.5B and shareholders will get an increased dividend. I

t will boost its investment to $80B over the next five years on organic growth projects in Australia, Chile and Canada. Moreover, the company is diversifying its energy portfolio by buying shale gas assets from Chesapeake Energy for $4.7B. Similarly, Rio Tinto’s net profit has almost tripled from $4.9B in 2009 to $14.3B in 2010. The company said it would return $5B to shareholders through a share buy-back programme by the end of 2012. We believe this is good news on the supply side as more companies will be in a better position to roll out new projects and increase production, though the impact on the copper market will not be felt for several years. #### Financial players are still in the price direction driving seat The price has been driven by continued recovery in consumption from the fundamentals, and financing deals in China sustaining imports and investor inflows in the rest of the world from financial influences. CRU expects the refined market to be very tight in Q2 and Q3, when we expect working stocks to hit bottom. In a market absent of financial players, we would expect prices to hit today’s levels only in Q3. However, financial influences are large in copper and have brought the rise in prices forward. Price direction in the short term remains in the hands of investment funds, particularly regarding the timing of their exit when they decide there is little more upside available. Over the next month we see prices trading sideways. A likely test of downside support at $9,200/t is supported by short term technical indicators. If breached then sub-$9,000/t is possible. The rebound in production last year recovered the losses in 2009, bringing output almost back to 2008 levels. The upturn in 2010 was driven by both a rebound in demand from end-use sectors, especially manufacturing, and restocking activity across the supply chain. North American output of copper alloy RBS advanced by 9.2% to 229,000t in 2010, a partial recovery from the 31.3% contraction in the previous year. US output amounted to 220,000t in 2010, up from 194,000t a year ago. US imports exhibited strong growth in 2010, particularly in Q4. With industrial production (IP) having increased by 5.7% in 2010, most of demand was from the industrial sector. Demand from the construction sector was sluggish as construction activity fell by a further 5.2% in 2010. Western European copper alloy RBS output totalled 864,000t in 2010, up by 23.7% from year ago levels. Italy, traditionally the largest producer in the region, saw output rise by 31.4% to 464,000t in 2010. Production continued to meet primarily local consumption needs. With the construction sector still depressed, demand was mainly supported by industrial applications. German output of copper alloy RBS increased by 38.6% to 194,000t in 2010. We estimate that German exports surged by almost 40% to 112,000t in 2010. Furthermore, demand from the domestic market significantly boosted production. Indeed, German construction activity, which is the healthiest in Western Europe, grew by 3.5% in 2010, while IP expanded by 10.1%. In particular, copper alloy RBS output benefited from robust German exports of industrial goods to developing regions. North East Asian output of copper alloy RBS rose by 19.8% to 497,000t in 2010. The highest

growth rate was exhibited in Japan, which had seen the steepest contraction in 2009.  Japanese output reached 191,000t in 2010, an increase of 25.3% from the previous year.  Japanese copper alloy RBS met mainly local market needs, with the upturn having been triggered by industrial applications.  Local construction activity fell by 5.8% in 2010.  South Korean copper alloy RBS production amounted to 214,000t in 2010, a 16.8% increase from 2009.  The number was also up from 201,000t in 2008.  South Korea exported 52,000t of copper alloy RBS in 2010, up from 37,000t a year ago.  Shipments to China, the USA and elsewhere increased noticeably in 2010. 

Chinese output of copper alloy RBS reached 890,000t in 2010, a 24.9% increase from the previous year. Production in China accounted for 30% of the world total in 2010, up from 24% two years ago.  Chinese copper alloy RBS output volume meets domestic requirements, though some of these final and intermediate goods are ultimately exported.  We estimate that Chinese consumption of copper alloy RBS by end use segment in 2010 was as follows: construction, 32%; electrical and electronic products, 15%; industrial machinery and equipment, 43%; HVACR, transportation and consumer general products, 10%. With such aggressive industrial development, it is not surprising that copper alloy RBS offtake saw a fast growth rate.  Chinese IP expanded by a remarkable 14.5% whilst construction activity soared by 17.8% in 2010. 

There is some migration from copper alloy RBS products towards copper alloy wire due to miniaturisation requirements in certain end use sectors.  We believe that the most vulnerable segments are electrical and electronic products (11% of world total copper alloy RBS demand), transportation (5%) and consumer general products (5%).  In the first and third groups, the principal driver is miniaturisation and lower weight.  In the second group, the main objective is lower weight, aimed to reduce fuel consumption.  Less exposure to escalating metal prices is an additional expected benefit for all segments.

## **Copper tube** 

Total production of copper tube increased by 12.6% to 2.4Mt in 2010.  We have emphasised that copper tube is one of the most vulnerable copper products, impacted by high and volatile copper prices and competing substitute products such as aluminium and plastic tubes.  This trend affects different regions in an uneven pattern, directed by operating costs and market growth rates. 

North America has suffered multi-year losses in copper tube production.  Copper tube output amounted to 336,000t in 2010, a 2.1% decline from the previous year.  US production fell by ‘only’ 1.7% to 277,000t in 2010 whilst that of Mexico contracted by 13.3% to 40,000t.  Obviously, this is to a large extent an outcome of the antidumping duties the US has imposed on all copper tube imports from

China and Mexico.  Interestingly, even though volumes are small, Canadian exports to the US have risen lately as some US importers have turned to Canada.  An important recent development was the announcement by **Golden Dragon** that it is considering establishing a copper commercial tube plant in the US, with three candidate locations being Thomasville, Ala., Little Rock, Ark. and Dallas, Tex.  Golden Dragon has established a plant in Mexico.  However, after the duties were imposed, it was more profitable to serve the US market from China rather than Mexico.  CRU understands that if Golden Dragon goes ahead with a US-located plant, the local copper tube industry will be significantly challenged. 

Western European copper tube output totalled 402,000t in 2010, up by 6.9% from the previous year. German output advanced by 23.3% to 153,000t in 2010.  Germany benefited from an increase both in domestic offtake and its traditional European markets.  Italian copper tube output increased by 19.0% to 70,000t in 2010, supported by a rebound in domestic consumption but primarily by stronger exports to European markets.  The market for copper tube in Western Europe remains a mixed picture, still impacted by the heavily troubled construction sector in many countries across the region. 

North East Asian copper tube output rose by 13.3% to 268,000t in 2010.  South Korea surpassed Japan to become the largest copper tube producer in the region.  South Korean exports grew strongly in 2010, with those to the US having more than doubled.  We understand that competitive South Korean copper tube fabricators must have benefited from the US antidumping duties on imports from China and Mexico. Japanese production reached 129,000t in 2010, up by 11.7% from 2009.  The rise in output met a stronger local market and increased exports to Malaysia. 

Chinese copper tube output expanded by 20.1% to 1.0Mt in 2010, accounting for 42% of the world total. That is impressive growth from a 35% share only two years ago.  Unsurprisingly, the US antidumping duties did have the expected big impact on Chinese copper tube exports.  Even though total Chinese shipments were only marginally down y-o-y in 2010, the share to the US fell from 32% in 2009 to 13% in 2010.  However, that loss was more than offset by uninterrupted domestic consumption growth and stronger demand from other overseas markets.  We estimate that Chinese copper tube fabricators' average capacity utilisation rate rose by 8% to 76% in 2010.  CRU was told that local demand for copper tube is still supported by a robust market for home appliances, which is triggered by an effective stimulus policy extended until the end of 2011.  The copper tube fabricators we spoke with were optimistic regarding market prospects in 2011 as they anticipate that the home appliance stimulus package will continue to support the market throughout the year. 

Not only is copper tube vulnerable to substitution, it is also vulnerable to rationing

# Industry News ## **Consumption** - The US **Copper and Brass Servicenter Association** expects that orders in Q1 2011 will increase despite the fall in December 2010. It was reported that 57% of service centres are expecting an increase in incoming orders over the next three months compared with Q4 2010, up from 44% in November 2010. However, promptness of payment may be an issue as 36% of service centres foresee payments to be less prompt in Q1 2011 compared to Q4 2010, up from 17% of respondents in November 2010. - It was reported that **Golden Dragon Precise Copper Tube Group** is considering establishing a copper commercial tube plant in the US. The three candidate locations are Thomasville, Ala., Little Rock, Ark. and Dallas, Tex. Golden Dragon’s copper tube products will serve the HVACR industry. This prospect comes further to the antidumping duties on copper tube imports from China and Mexico. Golden Dragon had established a tube factory in Mexico and its shipments to the US have been impacted due to the duties. © 2011 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 13 of 16 Copper Monitor March 2011 www.crumonitor.com - **Paranapanema** announced that it approved a capacity expansion and technology modernisation plan, supported by a positive macroeconomic outlook and favourable price trends for its products. The market will be boosted by Brazil’s anticipated economic growth, and in particular by infrastructure, civil construction, electricity and green power projects. In addition, the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympic Games will pro

vide further support.  Paranapanema will increase its refined copper capacity at its Dias D’Avila unit from 230,000t/y to 280,000t/y in H1 2012.  The company will also install a precious metal refining plant at the same unit, scheduled to be operational in H2 2012.  Paranapanema’s copper semis division, **Eluma** , will expand its cold rolling capacity from 28,000t/y to 55,000t/y.  Furthermore, hot rolled products capacity will rise from 60,000t/y to 200,000t/y whilst tube capacity double from 18,000t/y to 36,000t/y.  Investment of the entire plan for 2011-13 will amount to 630M reais (US$377M).

The Swedish copper wirerod producer commented that fabricators cannot act as bankers and have to shorten payment terms by nearly 50% compared to last year.  The company decided to reduce production of copper wirerod by 20% from 2010 in order to cut the stock level needed to be financed.  The main wirerod mill operations have gone down from four shifts to three. At the current copper price level, Elektrokoppar decided to cover the north European market rather than selling to other markets with high freight rates and high financing costs. 

- The **Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association** said that copper wire and cable shipments increased by 4.9% y-o-y to 56,600t in January 2011.  The association commented that although deliveries to the automotive sector were weak, those to the electric machinery sector were steady.  In addition, shipments to the construction industry were steady too after hitting the bottom. Shipments in January 2011 were the third lowest in the last 35 years, the lowest having been 2010 and 2009. 

- **Furukawa Electric** announced that it will triple its output capacity for copper foil used in lithium ion batteries to 1,500t per month in 2013.  The company will build a new factory with monthly capacity of 500t of foil in the western Taiwanese county of Yunlin.  Investment will amount to ¥6.9B and production is expected to begin in September 2012, gradually being brought up to speed by July 2013.  Furukawa Electric has a factory nearby that makes copper foil for circuit boards, and therefore it will be able to procure supplies for both.  In addition, the company said that electric power costs in Taiwan are half as expensive compared to Japan, and that will make it competitive in the growing segment of automotive lithium ion batteries.  Furukawa Electric will consider exporting foil for lithium ion batteries from Taiwan to China, South Korea and elsewhere.  Furthermore, ¥100M will be spent in order to revamp spare equipment at the existing copper foil factory in Nikko, Japan.  That will enable the plant to raise capacity by 80% to 1,000t per month by March 2012. 

- Chinese imports of refined copper and copper products increased to 364,420t in January 2011.  The numbers surpassed earlier expectations based on

the closed arbitrage window and the Chinese New Year festive season.  Imports were up by 5.7% from December 2010 and 24.7% from January 2010. Refined imports rose by 7.4% m-o-m to 245,617t but exports more than doubled to 23,193t, leaving net imports up by only 2% m-o-m.  The fact that Chinese copper buying was stronger than expected in the last three months implies that tightening monetary policies had little impact on copper demand.

The establishment will employ 360 and will be the third automotive connector production site in China, along with the plants in Tianjin and Huizhou.  In addition, SEI will construct a plant in Vietnam at a cost of ¥1.7B.  The facility will employ 430 and is anticipated to be

## **Mine Production** 







- In early February, Cyclone Yasi threatened copper and other metals production facilities in Australia’s North Queensland. **Xstrata** closed its copper refinery in **Townsville** for about two days and evacuated personnel at its **Mount Isa** mine and smelter. The Townsville refinery processes anode from the Mt Isa copper smelter and imported anode from Xstrata's **Altonorte** smelter in Chile. In addition, personnel at **Ernest Henry** mine was reduced to a handful employees for few days. Nevertheless, annual production will not be affected as there was no damage to these facilities. In 2010, Mount Isa and Ernest Henry produced 157,696t and 74,595t of copper-in-concentrate respectively, while Townsville produced some 287,000t of refined cathode. 

- In mid-February, unionised miners and management at **Codelco** ’s **Gaby** mine in Chile reached an agreement for a new collective labour contract. The negotiations started in January, well in advance of the expiration of the current agreement at the end of September 2011. The new contract includes a

4% pay increase and will last 44 months.  In 2010, Gaby produced around 112,000t of EW cathode. 

- **Inmet Mining Corporation** announced on 28<sup>th</sup> January that it had closed the previously announced transaction with **Ok Tedi Mining Limited** (OTML), whereby Inmet disposed of its 18% equity interest in OTML.  Inmet received gross proceeds of US$335 million which resulted in net proceeds received by Inmet of approximately US$307 million, after withholding taxes paid in Papua New Guinea (PNG).  The sale leaves Ok Tedi wholly owned by the PNG government.  In 2010, Ok Tedfi produced 160,000t of copper-in-concentrate. 

## **Exploration and Development** 



- **Equinox Minerals Limited** has announced that it plans to raise production at its **Lumwana** copper mine in Zambia to 260,000t/y from 147,000t/y in 2010.   A first stage feasibility study is due to be completed on the Lumwana expansion project by Q2 2011.  When this study commenced in early 2010, it was based on the resources defined at that time and was evaluating a plant expansion from the Lumwana plant nameplate capacity of 20Mt/y of ore to an increased capacity of 35Mt/y. However, as a consequence of the potential for a substantial increase in the Chimiwungo resource (the Chimiwungo East shoot was discovered in early 2010) and the upward shift in the outlook for copper prices, the study is now being conducted on the basis of a Chimiwungo mining inventory of 1 to 1.5Bt @0.6%Cu.  The assumed mining inventory would support a much larger scale operation with a throughput rate of 45Mt/y of ore and Lumwana would have a mine life in the range of 27 to 37 years. An expanded copper concentrator processing 45Mt/y of ore would produce approximately 260,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. The expansion of the concentrator (a replication of the existing Lumwana concentrator) is expected to cost around $450 - 550M.  The decision to expand is expected in early 2012 with expanded production anticipated to commence by 2015.  Ongoing expansion study activities will include completion of the resource drilling program, mine scheduling, mobile fleet studies, detailed design and costing of the plant expansion (including timing of a second crusher) and an evaluation of concentrate offtake scenarios.

## **Smelting and Refining** 



- Copper output at **Xstrata’s Kristiansand** copper-nickel electro-winning refinery in Norway was reduced to 60% from 4<sup>th</sup> February for around two weeks, following an explosion at the roaster that killed one worker. Calcine production was halted and production continued at a reduced rate using stocks of calcine.
